did_you_know.text: The biblical word zav is related to the root meaning “to flow” or “to drip.” It describes a continuing discharge, not an ordinary one-time event.
In this chapter, impurity can also be connected with objects such as a bed or seat. The rules therefore concern not only the person, but also contact and shared spaces.
The phrase “until evening” describes a temporary state: after washing and laundering, the person returns to normal status when evening arrives.
Even an accidental event such as spitting on a clean person is included in these rules. This shows that impurity does not necessarily depend on bad intentions.
A clay vessel touched by the zav is broken, while a wooden vessel is washed. The distinction likely reflects the porous nature of clay and the fact that wood can be rinsed.
“Living water” usually means flowing water, such as from a spring or stream, rather than water sitting in a container. In the Bible, such water is associated with freshness and life.
After becoming clean, the zav brings two turtledoves or two young pigeons rather than large animals. The purification ritual therefore uses relatively small offerings.
The chapter distinguishes an ordinary emission of semen, which causes impurity only until evening, from a continuing discharge. The waiting period and sacrifice are not the same.

A normal menstrual period is described here as lasting seven days, while bleeding that continues beyond its expected time receives stricter rules. The Bible therefore distinguishes a regular cycle from abnormal bleeding.
If a man has sexual relations with a woman during her menstrual period, he is also considered impure for seven days. This shows that the rules apply to both partners.
The stated purpose of separating from impurity is to protect the sanctuary located among the people. Impurity is presented as a concern for the whole community, not only for the individual.
